   21 |    * disk by the linear transformation
   22 |    *
   23 |    * [ dux duy ] [S] = [s]
   24 |    * [ dvx dvy ] [T] = [t]
   25 |    *
   26 |    * (The vector [S,T] is the difference between a position in output
   27 |    * space and [X,Y]; the vector [s,t] is the difference between a
   28 |    * position in input space and [x,y].)
   29 |    */
   30 |   /*
   31 |    * Output:
   32 |    *
   33 |    * major_mag is the half-length of the major axis of the "new"
   34 |    * ellipse.
   35 |    *
   36 |    * minor_mag is the half-length of the minor axis of the "new"
   37 |    * ellipse.
   38 |    *
   39 |    * major_unit_x is the x-coordinate of the major axis direction vector
   40 |    * of both the "old" and "new" ellipses.
   41 |    *
   42 |    * major_unit_y is the y-coordinate of the major axis direction vector.
   43 |    *
   44 |    * minor_unit_x is the x-coordinate of the minor axis direction vector.
   45 |    *
   46 |    * minor_unit_y is the y-coordinate of the minor axis direction vector.
   47 |    *
   48 |    * Unit vectors are useful for computing projections, in particular,
   49 |    * to compute the distance between a point in output space and the
   50 |    * center of a unit disk in output space, using the position of the
   51 |    * corresponding point [s,t] in input space. Following the clamping,
   52 |    * the square of this distance is
   53 |    *
   54 |    * ( ( s * major_unit_x + t * major_unit_y ) / major_mag )^2
   55 |    * +
   56 |    * ( ( s * minor_unit_x + t * minor_unit_y ) / minor_mag )^2
   57 |    *
   58 |    * If such distances will be computed for many [s,t]'s, it makes
   59 |    * sense to actually compute the reciprocal of major_mag and
   60 |    * minor_mag and multiply them by the above unit lengths.
   61 |    *
   62 |    * Now, if you want to modify the input pair of tangent vectors so
   63 |    * that it defines the modified ellipse, all you have to do is set
   64 |    *
   65 |    * newdux = major_mag * major_unit_x
   66 |    * newdvx = major_mag * major_unit_y
   67 |    * newduy = minor_mag * minor_unit_x = minor_mag * -major_unit_y
   68 |    * newdvy = minor_mag * minor_unit_y = minor_mag *  major_unit_x
   69 |    *
   70 |    * and use these tangent vectors as if they were the original ones.
   71 |    * Usually, this is a drastic change in the tangent vectors even if
   72 |    * the singular values are not clamped; for example, the minor axis
   73 |    * vector always points in a direction which is 90 degrees
   74 |    * counterclockwise from the direction of the major axis vector.
   75 |    */
   76 |   /*
   77 |    * Discussion:
   78 |    *
   79 |    * GOAL: Fix things so that the pullback, in input space, of a disk
   80 |    * of radius r in output space is an ellipse which contains, at
   81 |    * least, a disc of radius r. (Make this hold for any r>0.)
   82 |    *
   83 |    * ESSENCE OF THE METHOD: Compute the product of the first two
   84 |    * factors of an SVD of the linear transformation defining the
   85 |    * ellipse and make sure that both its columns have norm at least 1.
   86 |    * Because rotations and reflexions map disks to themselves, it is
   87 |    * not necessary to compute the third (rightmost) factor of the SVD.
   88 |    *
   89 |    * DETAILS: Find the singular values and (unit) left singular
   90 |    * vectors of Jinv, clampling up the singular values to 1, and
   91 |    * multiply the unit left singular vectors by the new singular
   92 |    * values in order to get the minor and major ellipse axis vectors.
   93 |    *
   94 |    * Image resampling context:
   95 |    *
   96 |    * The Jacobian matrix of the transformation at the output point
   97 |    * under consideration is defined as follows:
   98 |    *
   99 |    * Consider the transformation (x,y) -> (X,Y) from input locations
  100 |    * to output locations. (Anthony Thyssen, elsewhere in resample.c,
  101 |    * uses the notation (u,v) -> (x,y).)
  102 |    *
  103 |    * The Jacobian matrix of the transformation at (x,y) is equal to
  104 |    *
  105 |    *   J = [ A, B ] = [ dX/dx, dX/dy ]
  106 |    *       [ C, D ]   [ dY/dx, dY/dy ]
  107 |    *
  108 |    * that is, the vector [A,C] is the tangent vector corresponding to
  109 |    * input changes in the horizontal direction, and the vector [B,D]
  110 |    * is the tangent vector corresponding to input changes in the
  111 |    * vertical direction.
  112 |    *
  113 |    * In the context of resampling, it is natural to use the inverse
  114 |    * Jacobian matrix Jinv because resampling is generally performed by
  115 |    * pulling pixel locations in the output image back to locations in
  116 |    * the input image. Jinv is
  117 |    *
  118 |    *   Jinv = [ a, b ] = [ dx/dX, dx/dY ]
  119 |    *          [ c, d ]   [ dy/dX, dy/dY ]
  120 |    *
  121 |    * Note: Jinv can be computed from J with the following matrix
  122 |    * formula:
  123 |    *
  124 |    *   Jinv = 1/(A*D-B*C) [  D, -B ]
  125 |    *                      [ -C,  A ]
  126 |    *
  127 |    * What we do is modify Jinv so that it generates an ellipse which
  128 |    * is as close as possible to the original but which contains the
  129 |    * unit disk. This can be accomplished as follows:
  130 |    *
  131 |    * Let
  132 |    *
  133 |    *   Jinv = U Sigma V^T
  134 |    *
  135 |    * be an SVD decomposition of Jinv. (The SVD is not unique, but the
  136 |    * final ellipse does not depend on the particular SVD.)
  137 |    *
  138 |    * We could clamp up the entries of the diagonal matrix Sigma so
  139 |    * that they are at least 1, and then set
  140 |    *
  141 |    *   Jinv = U newSigma V^T.
  142 |    *
  143 |    * However, we do not need to compute V for the following reason:
  144 |    * V^T is an orthogonal matrix (that is, it represents a combination
  145 |    * of rotations and reflexions) so that it maps the unit circle to
  146 |    * itself. For this reason, the exact value of V does not affect the
  147 |    * final ellipse, and we can choose V to be the identity
  148 |    * matrix. This gives
  149 |    *
  150 |    *   Jinv = U newSigma.
  151 |    *
  152 |    * In the end, we return the two diagonal entries of newSigma
  153 |    * together with the two columns of U.
  154 |    */
  155 |   /*
  156 |    * ClampUpAxes was written by Nicolas Robidoux and Chantal Racette
  157 |    * of Laurentian University with insightful suggestions from Anthony
  158 |    * Thyssen and funding from the National Science and Engineering
  159 |    * Research Council of Canada. It is distinguished from its
  160 |    * predecessors by its efficient handling of degenerate cases.
  161 |    *
  162 |    * The idea of clamping up the EWA ellipse's major and minor axes so
  163 |    * that the result contains the reconstruction kernel filter support
  164 |    * is taken from Andreas Gustaffson's Masters thesis "Interactive
  165 |    * Image Warping", Helsinki University of Technology, Faculty of
  166 |    * Information Technology, 59 pages, 1993 (see Section 3.6).
  167 |    *
  168 |    * The use of the SVD to clamp up the singular values of the
  169 |    * Jacobian matrix of the pullback transformation for EWA resampling
  170 |    * is taken from the astrophysicist Craig DeForest.  It is
  171 |    * implemented in his PDL::Transform code (PDL = Perl Data
  172 |    * Language).
  173 |    */
  174 |   const double a = dux;
  175 |   const double b = duy;
  176 |   const double c = dvx;
  177 |   const double d = dvy;
  178 |   /*
  179 |    * n is the matrix Jinv * transpose(Jinv). Eigenvalues of n are the
  180 |    * squares of the singular values of Jinv.
  181 |    */
  182 |   const double aa = a*a;
  183 |   const double bb = b*b;
  184 |   const double cc = c*c;
  185 |   const double dd = d*d;
  186 |   /*
  187 |    * Eigenvectors of n are left singular vectors of Jinv.
  188 |    */
  189 |   const double n11 = aa+bb;
  190 |   const double n12 = a*c+b*d;
  191 |   const double n21 = n12;
  192 |   const double n22 = cc+dd;
  193 |   const double det = a*d-b*c;
  194 |   const double twice_det = det+det;
  195 |   const double frobenius_squared = n11+n22;
  196 |   const double discriminant =
  197 |     (frobenius_squared+twice_det)*(frobenius_squared-twice_det);
  198 |   /*
  199 |    * In exact arithmetic, discriminant can't be negative. In floating
  200 |    * point, it can, because of the bad conditioning of SVD
  201 |    * decompositions done through the associated normal matrix.
  202 |    */
  203 |   const double sqrt_discriminant =
  204 |     sqrt(discriminant > 0.0 ? discriminant : 0.0);
  205 |   /*
  206 |    * s1 is the largest singular value of the inverse Jacobian
  207 |    * matrix. In other words, its reciprocal is the smallest singular
  208 |    * value of the Jacobian matrix itself.
  209 |    * If s1 = 0, both singular values are 0, and any orthogonal pair of
  210 |    * left and right factors produces a singular decomposition of Jinv.
  211 |    */
  212 |   /*
  213 |    * Initially, we only compute the squares of the singular values.
  214 |    */
  215 |   const double s1s1 = 0.5*(frobenius_squared+sqrt_discriminant);
  216 |   /*
  217 |    * s2 the smallest singular value of the inverse Jacobian
  218 |    * matrix. Its reciprocal is the largest singular value of the
  219 |    * Jacobian matrix itself.
  220 |    */
  221 |   const double s2s2 = 0.5*(frobenius_squared-sqrt_discriminant);
  222 |   const double s1s1minusn11 = s1s1-n11;
  223 |   const double s1s1minusn22 = s1s1-n22;
  224 |   /*
  225 |    * u1, the first column of the U factor of a singular decomposition
  226 |    * of Jinv, is a (non-normalized) left singular vector corresponding
  227 |    * to s1. It has entries u11 and u21. We compute u1 from the fact
  228 |    * that it is an eigenvector of n corresponding to the eigenvalue
  229 |    * s1^2.
  230 |    */
  231 |   const double s1s1minusn11_squared = s1s1minusn11*s1s1minusn11;
  232 |   const double s1s1minusn22_squared = s1s1minusn22*s1s1minusn22;
  233 |   /*
  234 |    * The following selects the largest row of n-s1^2 I as the one
  235 |    * which is used to find the eigenvector. If both s1^2-n11 and
  236 |    * s1^2-n22 are zero, n-s1^2 I is the zero matrix.  In that case,
  237 |    * any vector is an eigenvector; in addition, norm below is equal to
  238 |    * zero, and, in exact arithmetic, this is the only case in which
  239 |    * norm = 0. So, setting u1 to the simple but arbitrary vector [1,0]
  240 |    * if norm = 0 safely takes care of all cases.
  241 |    */
  242 |   const double temp_u11 =
  243 |     ( (s1s1minusn11_squared>=s1s1minusn22_squared) ? n12 : s1s1minusn22 );
  244 |   const double temp_u21 =
  245 |     ( (s1s1minusn11_squared>=s1s1minusn22_squared) ? s1s1minusn11 : n21 );
  246 |   const double norm = sqrt(temp_u11*temp_u11+temp_u21*temp_u21);
  247 |   /*
  248 |    * Finalize the entries of first left singular vector (associated
  249 |    * with the largest singular value).
  250 |    */
  251 |   const double u11 = ( (norm>0.0) ? temp_u11/norm : 1.0 );
  252 |   const double u21 = ( (norm>0.0) ? temp_u21/norm : 0.0 );
  253 |   /*
  254 |    * Clamp the singular values up to 1.
  255 |    */
  256 |   *major_mag = ( (s1s1<=1.0) ? 1.0 : sqrt(s1s1) );
  257 |   *minor_mag = ( (s2s2<=1.0) ? 1.0 : sqrt(s2s2) );
  258 |   /*
  259 |    * Return the unit major and minor axis direction vectors.
  260 |    */
  261 |   *major_unit_x = u11;
  262 |   *major_unit_y = u21;
  263 |   *minor_unit_x = -u21;
  264 |   *minor_unit_y = u11;
  265 | }
